en: When Mayon Volcano erupts, flowing lava cools and solidifies into rock, gradually building up the mountain's cone over many eruptions.
During the southwest monsoon season, strong winds push moist air from the sea over the Philippines, causing heavy rainfall.
The continuous flow of the Cagayan River erodes soil and rocks over thousands of years, carving out its wide valley.
Tiny coral polyps in the Tubbataha Reefs extract calcium from seawater to build hard skeletons, slowly creating massive underwater structures.
Magma beneath Mount Makiling heats underground water into steam, which is then tapped to generate clean geothermal electricity.
Warm ocean waters in the Philippine Sea evaporate and rise, spinning into powerful typhoons due to the Earth's rotation.
Slightly acidic rainwater slowly dissolves the limestone bedrock in Palawan, carving out the massive Puerto Princesa Subterranean River over millennia.
Rainwater from the high mountains of Ifugao flows downward through an intricate canal system, naturally irrigating the stepped Banaue Rice Terraces.
The dense, tangled roots of coastal mangrove trees trap sediments and absorb wave energy, preventing shoreline erosion.
Taal Lake formed when a massive volcanic eruption emptied a magma chamber, causing the ground above it to collapse into a caldera.
Ocean currents deposit white sand and crushed corals onto shallow areas, gradually building up the long sandbars of Kalanggaman Island.
The gravitational pull of the moon and sun causes the water levels in Manila Bay to rise and fall daily, creating tides.
